title: Think in Comments — Plan the Job Before You Type Code

blocks.x: Goal

Plan a small robot battery report **in comments first**, then turn each comment into one line of arithmetic. The report answers four questions: how much voltage is usable, how long the pack should last, how much charge the test used, and what percentage is left.

items.x: **New ideas (max 2):**
**Comments are the plan:** Write the inputs, the output, the edge case and the expected check before typing code. A comment you cannot turn into one line is a question you have not answered yet.

**First draft, then test the edges:** Write the simplest version for the normal numbers, run it, then try a load that is too high and a run that is longer than the pack can supply. A program is finished when you can say which cases you checked.
**New syntax:** None. This lesson uses the variables and arithmetic from P.1 and P.2.
**Target time (unmeasured — [log yours](../.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/beginner-timing-log.md)):** Typical: 1.0–1.5 hours | Slow-learner: 1.5–2.0 hours

blocks.x: Requirements (what counts as complete)

**Key takeaway:** A comment that names the input, the output, the edge and the check is a plan you can turn into code one line at a time.

blocks.x: A beginner often opens the editor and starts typing because that feels like starting. Then the hard questions arrive halfway through: is the runtime based on the whole pack or only the usable part? Is “charge used” per hour or for this test? Should the answer be a voltage or a percentage? Each question forces a rewrite.
An engineer answers those questions **before** the code, in ordinary language:

blocks.text:
# Input: pack voltage, cutoff voltage, load current, capacity, run time.
# Output: usable voltage, estimated runtime, charge used, charge left.
# Edge: a load or run time that uses more than the pack holds.
# Check: the starter numbers should give 1300 mV, 314.3 min, 210 mAh and 90.5%.

blocks.x: Each line is a job you can finish:

items.x: **Input and output** decide which names exist and what each answer means. `runtime_min` is a duration, not a voltage.

**Edge** decides what you test after the normal case. A 30-minute run at 420 mA uses only 210 mAh of a 2200 mAh pack; a 10-hour run would use more than the pack has, so the report must not pretend otherwise.
**Check** gives you a concrete expected answer. Without it, “it ran” is the only thing you can say — and “it ran” is not the same as “it is right”.

blocks.x: The rule of thumb: **one comment, one line of code.** If a comment needs three lines, it is really two or three steps; split it. If a line has no comment above it, ask whether you can explain why it exists.
Idea 2: First draft, then make the edge fail

items.x: **Primary resource:** [Lesson P.1: Variables and Fundamental Data Types](P.1-variables-and-data-types.md)
**What to read:** how a name, a unit and a printed label are chosen before any arithmetic is written.
**What to skip:** the data-type catalogue; this lesson only needs plain numbers.
**Key takeaway:** A first draft is finished only when you have tried the normal case and the edge that would break it.

blocks.x: The first draft is allowed to be incomplete; it is not allowed to be vague. Write it in this order:

items.x: **Restate the problem in one sentence.** “Given a battery pack and a test load, report the usable voltage, runtime, charge used and charge left.”
**Name the pieces.** `pack_mv`, `cutoff_mv`, `load_ma`, `capacity_mah`, `run_minutes`.
**Write the steps as comments.** Subtract the cutoff. Divide capacity by load and convert hours to minutes. Multiply load by the run time. Subtract the charge used and divide by capacity.
**Turn each comment into code, top to bottom.** Run after each step, not after all of them.
**Try to break it.** A load of zero. A run time of zero. A run that uses the whole pack. A pack already at its cutoff.

blocks.x: Step 5 is where the learning happens. A program that passes the starter numbers is a hypothesis; the edge is the experiment. When an edge fails, you have found a question your plan did not answer — go back to the comments, answer it there, and only then change the code.

steps: Inputs: pack, cutoff, load, capacity, minutes
blocks.caption: Each box is a checkpoint in order; the last one is the verified pass this page ends on.
The plan in one line: inputs, four calculations, one checked output.

blocks.x: The five-step method: think, then type

The battery report is one instance of a method you will use on every P-track problem. It is not
about knowing the answer; it is about *earning* the answer in an order that keeps you honest.

items.x: **Restate the problem in one sentence, in your own words.** If you cannot, you are not ready to type. "Given a pack and a load, report four numbers about what the pack can do" is a restatement; "do the battery exercise" is not.

**Write down what you know and what you need.** Two columns: the given values with their units, and the answers with theirs. This is where a wrong unit — minutes against hours, mAh against mA — becomes visible while it still costs one word to fix.
**Plan in comments, one step per comment.** Each comment is a job: an input, a calculation, or a check. If a comment needs two verbs, split it. If a step has no comment, ask what it is for.

**Turn one comment into one line, then run it.** The first draft only has to be *honest*, not complete: normal numbers, the simplest arithmetic, run after every line so a wrong answer is one line away from the reason.

**Attack the plan, not the code.** Try the case you expect to break it: a load of zero, a run longer than the pack survives, a value already at the cutoff. When it breaks, the question you missed belongs in the comments — answer it there, then change the code.

blocks.x:
**What critical thinking looks like here.** At each step, ask three questions: *What do I know for
certain? What am I assuming? How would I find out?* The starter's names and units are facts. "The
runtime should be about five hours" is an assumption until `capacity / load` confirms it. The
expected output is how you find out. A learner who writes code first is answering those questions in
the wrong order, with the editor as a notepad.

**The first draft is allowed to be wrong; it is not allowed to be vague.** A draft with a comment
that says "work out the charge" has not decided anything. A draft that says "charge used = load
current × hours the test ran" has decided the units, the inputs and the shape of the line — and if
it is wrong, it is wrong in a place you can point at.
Bridge Notes

The same four comments work on every later P-track exercise. In P.3 the input is a raw command, the output is a clamped command, the edge is a value outside 0–255, and the check is the boundary case you can work out by hand. Writing those four lines first turns a page of instructions into a short list of jobs.

The battery report shows why the plan is written before the formulas. Each answer has a unit, and the unit decides the arithmetic: runtime is minutes, so hours from the charge-and-current pair must be scaled; charge used is mAh, so the run time must be in hours. A learner who starts typing formulas meets those choices halfway through the file, when the names are already fixed and a wrong unit looks like a wrong number. A learner who writes the four comments first meets them on paper, where a change costs one line.

The comments are also the debugging order: when the answer is wrong, you can ask which comment failed instead of rereading the whole program. A first draft in comments is cheap to change — moving a step or adding the edge is one line of prose, not a rewrite of working code. Keep the four lines at the top of the file as the record of what you checked.

blocks.x: Hint Ladder

Write the units beside each answer before writing the formula. Runtime is minutes, so `capacity_mah / load_ma` gives hours and must be multiplied by 60. Charge used is in mAh, so the run time must be in hours: `run_minutes / 60`.

blocks.text:
usable_mv = pack_mv - cutoff_mv
runtime_min = (capacity_mah / load_ma) * 60
charge_used_mah = load_ma * (run_minutes / 60)
charge_left_percent = ((capacity_mah - charge_used_mah) / capacity_mah) * 100

blocks.x: Common mistakes & troubleshooting

items.x: **Runtime in hours instead of minutes:** `capacity_mah / load_ma` gives hours. Multiply by 60 before printing minutes.
**Charge used without converting minutes to hours:** `load_ma * run_minutes` is 100 times too large. Use `run_minutes / 60`.
**Percentage as a fraction:** `(capacity - used) / capacity` gives 0.905, not 90.5. Multiply by 100 for a percentage.
**Typing the expected answer:** The grader changes the inputs. Compute from the names, never from the output block.

blocks.x: Check yourself

items.x: **Why is `runtime_min` based on `capacity_mah / load_ma` and not on the usable voltage?**

blocks.x: Capacity is charge, measured in mAh; load is current, measured in mA. Dividing charge by current gives time. The usable voltage is a separate fact about the pack's safe range, not the amount of charge it holds.

items.x: **A run uses 210 mAh of a 2200 mAh pack. What percentage is left, and why is that not 9.5%?**
